p01-l01.principle: It becomes negative because it has more electrons than protons.
p01-l01.reasoning: Protons carry positive charge and electrons carry an equal magnitude of negative charge. A neutral atom has equal numbers of both. Adding an electron leaves an excess of negative charge.
p01-l01.application: Static charging transfers electrons between materials. A surface that gains electrons becomes negatively charged without requiring its nuclei to move.
p01-l01.distinction: Particle count and net charge are different: the sign of the added particle matters.

p01-l01.principle: Mobile electrons drift through a structure whose positive ion cores stay in place.
p01-l01.reasoning: A metal has electrons that can move through its structure. Its positive ion cores remain arranged in the solid, vibrating around their positions. A small average drift of mobile electrons produces current.
p01-l01.application: A fixed copper conductor transfers charge while remaining mechanically secured in its terminals.
p01-l01.distinction: Charge movement through a solid does not mean the solid itself flows.

p01-l01.principle: Conduction electrons that can move through the metal.
p01-l01.reasoning: Some electrons in copper are mobile within the metallic structure. An electric field produces an average drift of these negatively charged carriers. The positive ion cores remain part of the solid.
p01-l01.application: A copper cable and a battery electrolyte both carry current, but the moving charge carriers are different.
p01-l01.distinction: The charge carrier depends on the material; metallic conduction is electron conduction.

p01-l01.principle: Their charges have equal magnitude but opposite signs.
p01-l01.reasoning: A proton carries positive elementary charge and an electron carries an equal magnitude of negative charge. Their different masses do not change this equality, which explains how equal numbers can give a neutral atom.
p01-l01.application: Use the particle model to explain electrical neutrality before considering charge transfer between materials.
p01-l01.distinction: Charge magnitude, charge sign and particle mass are separate properties.

p01-l01.reasoning: An electron carries negative charge, so adding one makes the net charge more negative.
p01-l01.application: A copper cable conducts because some electrons can move through its structure. The cable does not need to supply a new batch of electrons whenever an appliance starts.
p01-l01.distinction: A practical action is justified by the circuit condition and intended evidence, not by a familiar sequence alone.

p01-l02.principle: Some electrons are mobile throughout the metal while its ion cores remain in place.
p01-l02.reasoning: Copper has mobile conduction electrons distributed throughout its structure. An electric field gives their motion a small average drift. Copper therefore conducts without its solid structure travelling through the circuit.
p01-l02.application: A copper cable can carry current continuously while remaining fixed inside a wall and at its terminals.
p01-l02.distinction: The electrons are mobile; the copper structure stays in place.

p01-l02.principle: Charges already present throughout the circuit respond as the electric field change propagates.
p01-l02.reasoning: Mobile charges are already distributed through the conductors. Closing the circuit changes the electric field, and that change propagates rapidly through the circuit. The charges respond locally, so the lamp need not wait for a particular electron from the source.
p01-l02.application: A long lighting circuit can respond promptly even though any one electron has moved only a small average distance.
p01-l02.distinction: Electron drift is motion of individual charge carriers. Signal propagation is the spread of an electrical change.

p01-l02.principle: Left to right, because conventional current follows positive-charge movement.
p01-l02.reasoning: An electron has negative charge. Its movement therefore produces conventional current in the opposite direction. Circuit diagrams use this positive-charge convention consistently.
p01-l02.application: Use conventional current arrows consistently when interpreting circuit diagrams and magnetic-field rules.
p01-l02.distinction: A current arrow is a reference for charge flow, not a picture of an electron’s path.

p01-l02.principle: It helps explain mobile electrons moving through the metal without the nuclei travelling with them.
p01-l02.reasoning: The instructor’s outer-shell model introduces why some electrons are mobile in copper. In the solid, these conduction electrons can move through the metallic structure while its positive ion cores remain essentially in place.
p01-l02.application: This is the model behind a mechanically fixed conductor carrying current.
p01-l02.distinction: Movement of charge through copper does not require movement of the copper structure.

p01-l02.principle: It is neutral because the positive and negative charges balance.
p01-l02.reasoning: Each proton contributes positive charge and each electron an equal magnitude of negative charge. With equal counts, their net contribution is zero. The outer electron’s mobility is a separate property.
p01-l02.application: Keep the explanation of copper’s neutrality separate from the explanation of its conductivity.
p01-l02.distinction: Neutral does not mean unable to conduct; it means zero net charge.

p01-l03.principle: An increase in negative charge by a whole-number multiple of the elementary charge.
p01-l03.reasoning: Each electron carries the same fixed magnitude of charge. Ordinary charging transfers electrons, so the net change comes in whole multiples of that magnitude. Very large numbers make charge appear continuous in installation calculations.
p01-l03.application: An ammeter reports a macroscopic flow rate; it does not need to count each electron individually.
p01-l03.distinction: A practically smooth current can still be carried by discrete particles.

p01-l03.principle: The amount of transferred charge; elapsed time is still needed to find average current.
p01-l03.reasoning: The coulomb measures charge amount. It does not include time or energy. Current needs charge divided by elapsed time; energy transferred per charge depends on voltage.
p01-l03.application: A charge figure alone cannot tell you whether a cable has carried a small current for a long time or a large current briefly.
p01-l03.distinction: C measures charge; A measures charge per second; J measures energy.

p01-l03.reasoning: The prefix milli means one thousandth of the base unit. Therefore 30 milliamperes is 30 divided by 1,000 amperes. The physical current stays the same when its unit notation changes.
p01-l03.application: Residual-current ratings often use mA while load-current ratings use A. Convert the units before comparing numerical values.
p01-l03.distinction: A prefix changes the scale of the number, not the electrical quantity.

p01-l03.principle: An amount of electric charge, without by itself stating the transfer time.
p01-l03.reasoning: The coulomb gives a practical unit for an amount of electric charge. A time interval is additionally needed to calculate the average current associated with a transfer of that charge.
p01-l03.application: When reading a charge-transfer example, keep the coulomb value and the elapsed time as separate inputs.
p01-l03.distinction: Charge is an amount; current is a rate.

p01-l03.reasoning: Milli means one thousandth: 1 A = 1,000 mA.

p01-l03.distinction: A practical action is justified by the circuit condition and intended evidence, not by a familiar sequence alone.

p01-l04.principle: One coulomb of charge passes that point each second.
p01-l04.reasoning: Current is the rate of charge transfer. One ampere means one coulomb passes a point in each second. A current value therefore always includes an amount-per-time relationship.
p01-l04.application: A steady 2 A transfers 10 C past a point in 5 s. The conductor does not accumulate all that charge at the measuring point.
p01-l04.distinction: Charge is how much; current is how much per second.

p01-l04.principle: The first carries twice the average current: 4 A compared with 2 A.
p01-l04.reasoning: Average current is transferred charge divided by elapsed time. With the same charge, halving the time doubles the average current. Calculate each rate using the same units before comparing.
p01-l04.application: A brief high-current pulse and a longer low-current supply can transfer the same charge while imposing different heating conditions.
p01-l04.distinction: Total charge can be equal even when current differs.

p01-l04.reasoning: Two amperes means two coulombs each second. Five seconds therefore transfers five lots of two coulombs. Multiplying current by time gives charge when the current is steady.

p01-l04.reasoning: The current is 12/4 = 3 A. At this unchanged rate, 8 s transfers 3 × 8 = 24 C. A fixed current does not mean a fixed total charge over increasingly long intervals.
p01-l04.application: Use elapsed time with the measured current when estimating transferred charge.

p01-l04.principle: The rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes.
p01-l04.reasoning: Charge is an amount, measured in coulombs. Current is how quickly charge passes a point, measured in amperes. One ampere means one coulomb passes each second, so both the amount and the time matter.
p01-l04.application: If 6 coulombs pass a point in 2 seconds, the average current is 3 amperes. The same charge taking longer would mean a smaller average current.
p01-l04.distinction: Current must be distinguished from Line and phase values; they do not name the same electrical quantity or function.
